headline: UNICEF Chief Urges Bangladesh to End Child Marriage
meta_description: UN children's agency calls for urgent investment to keep girls in school and end child marriage in Bangladesh, where nearly half of young women wed before 18.
summary_short: UNICEF's executive director visited Bangladesh to push for action on child marriage, girls' education, and refugee children's learning amid rising humanitarian needs.
body:
Nearly half of young women in Bangladesh are married before age 18—a reality that prompted the UN children's agency to launch an urgent call for change this week. During a three-day visit, UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell heard directly from adolescent girls in Korail, Dhaka's largest informal settlement, about the pressures that force them out of school and into early marriage. According to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025, 47.2 per cent of women aged 20 to 24 were married before reaching adulthood. Russell urged the Government to close legal loopholes that permit child marriage and to ensure girls complete secondary education—a path that protects them from exploitation, trafficking, and foreclosed futures.

Meeting with senior officials, Russell welcomed Bangladesh's commitment to increase spending on education and health to five per cent of the country's gross domestic product. "Budgets reflect priorities," she said, stressing that turning promises into concrete investment is essential. Beyond domestic reform, Russell travelled to Cox's Bazar, where she visited UNICEF-supported learning centres serving Rohingya refugee children in one of the world's largest refugee camps. She emphasized that education shields vulnerable children from armed group recruitment and trafficking—services that are increasingly at risk as humanitarian funding declines globally.

Recognizing Bangladesh's generosity in hosting the refugee population, Russell appealed to the international community to sustain support for both Rohingya and host-community children. As resources shrink, she warned, the risk grows that the most vulnerable will be left behind. The message was clear: investing in children's education, health, nutrition, and protection is not charity—it is investing in Bangladesh's future.
quick_facts: 47.2% of Bangladeshi women aged 20-24 married before age 18
UNICEF chief visited Korail, Dhaka's largest informal settlement
Bangladesh hosts one of world's largest refugee camps in Cox's Bazar
Government committed to 5% GDP spending on education and health
Education protects children from trafficking, exploitation, and armed recruitment
